CHAPTER 31 — FOOD PRODUCTION

Introduction

Food is one of the most basic needs of every living being. India is one of the most populous countries in the world, and its population continues to grow. To feed this ever-increasing number of people, the country must produce more and more food every year. At the same time the land available for farming is limited and is even shrinking as towns and industries expand. Therefore, the only practical way to meet the growing demand is to obtain MORE food from the SAME (or less) land — that is, to increase the YIELD per unit area. This chapter explains the scientific methods used to raise food production from both plants (crop production) and animals (animal husbandry), together with the management practices, crop protection, sustainable farming and food-preservation techniques that make a reliable food supply possible.

31.1 THE NEED TO INCREASE FOOD PRODUCTION

When the population grows, the demand for food grows with it. Before independence India often had to import food grains. After independence the country set out to become self-sufficient in food. Simply bringing more land under the plough is not enough, because good agricultural land is limited. The scientific solution is to increase PRODUCTIVITY — the amount of grain produced per hectare. This is achieved by:
 - growing improved (high-yielding) varieties of crops,
 - supplying the right nutrients through manures and fertilisers,
 - providing assured irrigation,
 - protecting crops from weeds, pests and diseases, and
 - storing the harvested produce safely so that it is not lost.

THE GREEN REVOLUTION
During the 1960s, India introduced HIGH-YIELDING VARIETIES (HYVs) of wheat and rice, together with chemical fertilisers, assured irrigation and modern farm machinery. This package of practices dramatically raised the production of food grains and made India self-sufficient in cereals. This great increase in food-grain production is called the GREEN REVOLUTION. Similar large increases in milk production (the WHITE REVOLUTION or Operation Flood) and in fish production (the BLUE REVOLUTION) have followed in animal husbandry and fisheries.

31.2 CROP PRODUCTION AND MANAGEMENT

(a) Crop variety improvement
A high-yielding crop variety gives more produce of better quality from the same area. New varieties are produced mainly by:
 - HYBRIDISATION — crossing two genetically different but desirable parent plants so that the offspring (the hybrid) combines the good qualities of both, such as high yield, disease resistance and drought tolerance. Crossing may be between different varieties (intervarietal), different species (interspecific) or different genera (intergeneric).
 - SELECTION — choosing the best plants from a population and using their seeds for the next crop.
Desirable features sought in improved varieties include high yield, resistance to disease and pests, tolerance to drought or flooding (so the crop survives bad weather), early maturity (so more crops can be grown in a year), and good nutritional quality.

(b) Crop seasons
In India crops are grown in two main seasons:
 - KHARIF crops are sown at the beginning of the rainy (monsoon) season around June–July and harvested around September–October. Examples: rice (paddy), maize, soyabean, groundnut, cotton.
 - RABI crops are sown in the winter around October–November and harvested in spring around March–April. Examples: wheat, gram, peas, mustard, barley.

(c) Nutrient management
Plants need NUTRIENTS to grow. Sixteen elements are essential; air and water supply carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, while the soil supplies the rest. The three nutrients that plants need in the largest amounts are NITROGEN (N), PHOSPHORUS (P) and POTASSIUM (K) — together called the macronutrients, or simply NPK. These can be supplied in two ways:

MANURES are decomposed organic matter made from animal dung, urine, plant waste and farm refuse. Compost and farmyard manure are common examples. Manures contain small amounts of nutrients but large amounts of organic matter.
 Advantages of manures: they add HUMUS, which improves soil texture, water-holding capacity and aeration; they encourage useful soil micro-organisms; they are cheap and use up farm waste; and they are environmentally friendly.
 Disadvantage: they contain only small quantities of nutrients, so large amounts must be applied.

FERTILISERS are commercially produced chemical substances rich in a particular nutrient — for example urea and ammonium sulphate supply nitrogen, superphosphate supplies phosphorus, and muriate of potash supplies potassium. NPK fertilisers supply all three together.
 Advantages of fertilisers: they are rich in nutrients, so small quantities give a large effect; they are easy to store, transport and apply; and they give quick, high yields.
 Disadvantages of fertilisers: they are costly; their continued use without manure damages soil structure and reduces soil fertility; excess fertiliser washed into ponds and rivers causes water pollution and the over-growth of algae (eutrophication).
A balanced approach uses BOTH manures (to maintain soil health) and fertilisers (for high yield).

(d) Irrigation
Most crops need a regular and assured supply of water. Supplying water to fields by artificial means is called IRRIGATION. Sources of irrigation water include wells and tube-wells, canals, rivers, tanks and dams. Common methods are:
 - the moat or pulley system and modern pumps to lift well water,
 - canal and river-lift systems,
 - and modern water-saving methods such as SPRINKLER systems (water sprayed like rain, useful on sandy or uneven land) and DRIP irrigation (water delivered drop by drop directly to the roots, which saves the most water and is ideal for orchards and water-scarce regions).

(e) Cropping patterns
Farmers arrange their crops in patterns that make the best use of land, water and nutrients:
 - MIXED CROPPING: growing two or more crops together on the same field at the same time (for example wheat with gram). This reduces the risk of total failure — if one crop fails the other may survive.
 - INTERCROPPING: growing two or more crops in the same field in a definite pattern of rows. This makes better use of sunlight and nutrients and helps control pests.
 - CROP ROTATION: growing different crops on the same field in a planned sequence across seasons. Growing a leguminous (pulse) crop, whose root nodules fix atmospheric nitrogen, restores soil fertility for the next cereal crop and reduces the build-up of pests and diseases.

31.3 CROP PROTECTION AND STORAGE

Crops can be damaged before and after harvest. The main enemies of crops are:
 - WEEDS: unwanted plants (such as wild oats and amaranthus) that grow with the crop and compete for water, nutrients, light and space, lowering the yield. Weeds are controlled mechanically (by hand-weeding, hoeing and ploughing) and chemically (using WEEDICIDES such as 2,4-D).
 - INSECT PESTS: insects that attack roots, stems, leaves, flowers or fruits, or suck the plant's sap. They are controlled using INSECTICIDES.
 - DISEASES: caused by pathogens such as bacteria, fungi and viruses present in the soil, water or air. They are controlled by treating seeds, using disease-resistant varieties, and applying fungicides and other PESTICIDES.

Pesticides (a general term covering insecticides, weedicides and fungicides) protect crops but cause serious problems if overused: they pollute the soil and water, kill useful insects such as bees and friendly soil organisms, leave harmful residues on food, and can harm the health of farm workers and consumers. Their excessive use also leads to pests becoming resistant. Hence they must be used carefully and sparingly, and biological methods of control are encouraged.

STORAGE OF GRAINS
A large part of the harvest can be lost in storage. Losses are caused by BIOTIC factors (insects, rodents, mites, fungi and bacteria) and ABIOTIC factors (inappropriate moisture and temperature). To prevent these losses the grain is first DRIED so that its moisture content is low, then cleaned, and stored in clean, dry, airtight containers, godowns or silos. Fumigants are used to kill pests. Proper drying and storage preserve both the quantity and the quality (germination capacity) of the grain.

31.4 ANIMAL HUSBANDRY

The scientific management and rearing of useful animals for food and other products is called ANIMAL HUSBANDRY. It covers cattle, poultry, fish and bees.

(a) Cattle farming
Cattle (cows and buffaloes) are reared for two main purposes:
 - MILCH animals (dairy animals) are kept for MILK. Good milch breeds of cow include Red Sindhi and Sahiwal; high-milk exotic breeds include Jersey and Holstein-Friesian. Buffaloes such as Murrah are excellent milk producers. Crossing Indian breeds with exotic breeds combines disease resistance with high milk yield.
 - DRAUGHT animals are used for farm work such as ploughing, drawing carts and irrigation.
Good cattle management requires clean, well-ventilated, dry shelters; regular grooming and brushing; and a balanced diet of FODDER. Fodder has two parts: ROUGHAGE (fibre-rich food such as hay and straw) and CONCENTRATES (nutrient-rich food such as oil cakes and grains). Care must also be taken to prevent and treat diseases through vaccination and hygiene.

(b) Poultry farming
POULTRY FARMING is the rearing of domestic fowl (chickens, ducks, etc.) for eggs and meat. Birds reared mainly for EGGS are called LAYERS, and those reared mainly for MEAT are called BROILERS. Broilers are fed protein- and fat-rich diets so that they grow quickly, while layers need diets rich in nutrients for egg production. Poultry needs clean housing, the right temperature and lighting, balanced feed and protection from diseases such as bird flu through vaccination and hygiene.

(c) Fish production
Fish is an important and cheap source of animal PROTEIN. Fish are obtained in two ways:
 - CAPTURE FISHERIES: catching fish from natural water bodies such as seas, rivers and lakes. Marine (sea) fishing uses boats and nets, and shoals of fish are often located using satellites and echo-sounders.
 - CULTURE FISHERIES (fish farming): the controlled rearing of fish in ponds and tanks. Rearing aquatic organisms (fish, prawns, etc.) under controlled conditions is called AQUACULTURE, and the rearing of fish in particular is called PISCICULTURE. In COMPOSITE FISH CULTURE several compatible species that feed at different levels of the pond (surface, middle and bottom feeders) are reared together so that all the food in the pond is used and the yield is high.

(d) Bee-keeping (apiculture)
The rearing of honey-bees in artificial hives to obtain honey and wax is called APICULTURE or bee-keeping. Bees are kept in box-like hives placed near fields and orchards. The bees collect nectar from flowers and convert it into HONEY, which is a nutritious, easily digestible food and is also used in medicine. Bees also produce BEESWAX, used in many products. Importantly, while collecting nectar the bees POLLINATE the flowers, which increases the yield of crops and fruits. The Italian bee (Apis mellifera) is commonly reared for its high honey yield and gentle nature.

31.5 SUSTAINABLE AGRICULTURE AND ORGANIC FARMING

Heavy use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides raises yields in the short term but harms the soil, water and human health in the long term. SUSTAINABLE AGRICULTURE aims to produce enough food for the present without damaging the environment or reducing the ability of future generations to grow food. It relies on mixed cropping, crop rotation, integrated pest management, water conservation and the use of organic manures.
ORGANIC FARMING is a system of farming that avoids or greatly limits synthetic fertilisers and pesticides. Instead it uses organic manures (compost, farmyard manure, green manure and vermicompost), bio-fertilisers, biological pest control (using natural predators) and crop rotation. Organic farming keeps the soil fertile and alive, produces chemical-free food and protects the environment, though yields may be somewhat lower and the produce is often costlier.

31.6 FOOD PRESERVATION

Food spoils mainly because of the action of micro-organisms (bacteria, fungi and yeasts) and because of enzymes, moisture, air and heat. FOOD PRESERVATION means treating and storing food so that it does not spoil and can be kept and used for a longer time. Common methods are:
 - DRYING (dehydration): removing water from food (for example, drying grains, pulses, fish, and making raisins from grapes). Micro-organisms cannot grow without moisture.
 - SALTING (and use of sugar): adding salt or sugar draws water out of the food and out of microbial cells, preventing their growth. Pickles, salted fish and jams are preserved this way.
 - CANNING: cooking food, sealing it in airtight cans or bottles, and heating it to kill micro-organisms. Sealed canned food keeps for a long time.
 - REFRIGERATION AND FREEZING: storing food at low temperature slows the growth of micro-organisms and the action of enzymes, keeping food such as milk, vegetables, meat and fish fresh.
Other methods include the use of chemical preservatives (such as salts of benzoic and sorbic acid), boiling and pasteurisation (for milk).

SUMMARY

- A growing population needs more food, but farmland is limited; so productivity (yield per hectare) must be raised by scientific methods.
- The Green Revolution used high-yielding varieties, fertilisers and irrigation to make India self-sufficient in food grains.
- Crop variety improvement uses hybridisation and selection to obtain high-yielding, disease-resistant, early-maturing varieties.
- Crops are grown in two seasons: kharif (monsoon) and rabi (winter).
- Nutrients are supplied by manures (organic, improve soil) and fertilisers (chemical, rich in NPK, give quick yield); a balance of both is best.
- Irrigation supplies water; sprinkler and drip methods save water.
- Cropping patterns — mixed cropping, intercropping and crop rotation — make better use of land and reduce risk; legumes in rotation restore soil nitrogen.
- Crops are protected from weeds, insect pests and diseases; pesticides help but pollute and must be used carefully. Grain must be dried and stored properly.
- Animal husbandry includes cattle farming (milch and draught animals), poultry farming (layers and broilers), fish production (capture and culture fisheries) and bee-keeping (apiculture).
- Sustainable and organic farming protect soil, water and health for the future.
- Food is preserved by drying, salting, canning and refrigeration so that it lasts longer.

chapter_summary.title: Food Production — Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Class 10 Science & Technology (212) Learner's Guide summary for Lesson 31. It explains why food production must increase for a growing population, the methods of crop production and management (variety improvement, nutrient management, irrigation, cropping patterns), crop protection and storage, animal husbandry (cattle, poultry, fisheries and bee-keeping), and sustainable farming and food preservation.

sections.heading: Need to increase food production and the Green Revolution
bullets: The population keeps growing while farmland is limited, so the yield of food per hectare must be increased by scientific methods.
The Green Revolution of the 1960s introduced high-yielding varieties (HYVs) of wheat and rice with fertilisers, irrigation and machinery, making India self-sufficient in food grains.
Similar increases gave the White Revolution (milk) and the Blue Revolution (fish).

sections.heading: Crop variety improvement and nutrient management
bullets: Improved varieties are produced by hybridisation (crossing two desirable parents) and selection; they are high-yielding, disease-resistant, early-maturing and drought-tolerant.
Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium (NPK) are the macronutrients needed in the largest amounts.
Manures are organic, add humus and improve the soil but are nutrient-poor; fertilisers are chemical, nutrient-rich and give quick yield but can harm the soil and pollute water if overused.
A balanced use of both manures and fertilisers is best for the soil and the crop.

sections.heading: Cropping patterns and irrigation
bullets: Kharif crops (rice, maize, cotton) are grown in the rainy season; rabi crops (wheat, gram, mustard) are grown in winter.
Mixed cropping grows two crops together to reduce risk; intercropping grows them in a row pattern; crop rotation grows different crops in sequence to restore fertility (legumes fix nitrogen).
Irrigation supplies water from wells, canals, tanks and dams; sprinkler and drip systems save water.

sections.heading: Crop protection and storage
bullets: Weeds compete with crops and are removed by weeding or weedicides; insect pests are controlled by insecticides; diseases (by bacteria, fungi, viruses) are controlled by resistant varieties and fungicides.
Pesticides protect crops but pollute soil and water, kill useful insects and leave harmful residues, so they must be used sparingly.
Harvested grain must be dried to low moisture and stored in clean, dry, airtight godowns or silos to prevent loss from insects, rodents and fungi.

sections.heading: Animal husbandry, sustainable farming and food preservation
bullets: Cattle are reared as milch (milk) or draught (work) animals and need clean shelter and balanced fodder (roughage + concentrates); poultry are reared as layers (eggs) or broilers (meat).
Fish are obtained by capture fisheries (natural waters) and culture fisheries/aquaculture (ponds); bee-keeping (apiculture) gives honey and wax and helps pollinate crops.
Sustainable and organic farming protect the soil and environment; food is preserved by drying, salting, canning and refrigeration.

key_takeaways: Food production must be increased because the population is growing while farmland is limited; the answer is higher yield per hectare.
The Green Revolution used HYVs, fertilisers and irrigation to make India self-sufficient in food grains.
Manures improve soil health; fertilisers (NPK) give quick high yields but pollute if overused — a balance of both is best.
Kharif (monsoon) and rabi (winter) are the two crop seasons; mixed cropping, intercropping and crop rotation make better use of land and reduce risk.
Pesticides protect crops from weeds, pests and diseases but must be used carefully; grain must be dried and stored safely.
Animal husbandry covers cattle (milch/draught), poultry (layers/broilers), fish (capture/culture fisheries) and bee-keeping (apiculture).
Sustainable and organic farming protect the environment, and food is preserved by drying, salting, canning and refrigeration.

worksheet.title: Worksheet — Food Production (NIOS Official)
worksheet.instructions: This is the NIOS Secondary Science & Technology (212) official Worksheet-31 for Lesson 31. Attempt all questions. Support your answers with examples from Indian agriculture and animal husbandry where appropriate.

questions.question: Why is it necessary to increase food production in India? Give two reasons.
questions.answer: India's population is large and continues to grow, so the demand for food rises every year, while the land available for farming is limited and is shrinking as towns and industries expand. (1) Growing population means more mouths to feed, so total food output must rise. (2) Because good farmland cannot be increased much, the only practical way is to raise the YIELD per hectare (productivity) using improved varieties, fertilisers, irrigation and crop protection — rather than simply clearing more land.
questions.explanation: Growing population + limited land → must raise productivity per hectare.

questions.question: What was the Green Revolution? State its main components.
questions.answer: The Green Revolution was the great increase in food-grain (mainly wheat and rice) production in India that began in the 1960s and made the country self-sufficient in cereals. Its main components were: (i) high-yielding varieties (HYVs) of seeds, (ii) chemical fertilisers (NPK), (iii) assured irrigation, (iv) modern farm machinery, and (v) crop protection with pesticides. Together this package of practices raised the yield per hectare dramatically.
questions.explanation: Definition + HYVs, fertilisers, irrigation, machinery, pesticides.

questions.question: Differentiate between manures and fertilisers (any three points).
questions.answer: Manure: (1) is decomposed organic matter from animal dung and plant/farm waste; (2) contains small amounts of nutrients but plenty of humus, so it improves soil texture, water-holding capacity and aeration; (3) is cheap and environmentally friendly. Fertiliser: (1) is a commercially produced chemical substance (e.g. urea, superphosphate); (2) is rich in a particular nutrient, so a small quantity gives a big effect and quick high yield; (3) is costly and, if overused without manure, damages soil structure and pollutes water. In short, manures feed the SOIL while fertilisers feed the CROP.
questions.explanation: Organic vs chemical; nutrient-poor + humus vs nutrient-rich; cheap/eco vs costly/polluting.

questions.question: Distinguish between kharif and rabi crops with two examples each.
questions.answer: KHARIF crops are sown at the beginning of the rainy/monsoon season (June–July) and harvested in September–October; they need warm, wet weather. Examples: rice (paddy) and maize (also cotton, soyabean, groundnut). RABI crops are sown in winter (October–November) and harvested in spring (March–April); they need cool growing weather and mild warmth at harvest. Examples: wheat and gram (also peas, mustard, barley).
questions.explanation: Kharif = monsoon-sown (rice, maize); rabi = winter-sown (wheat, gram).

questions.question: Explain mixed cropping, intercropping and crop rotation. How does crop rotation help maintain soil fertility?
questions.answer: MIXED CROPPING is growing two or more crops together on the same field at the same time without a fixed row pattern (e.g. wheat + gram). If one crop fails, the other may survive, so it reduces the risk of total loss. INTERCROPPING is growing two or more crops in the same field in a definite pattern of rows (e.g. a few rows of one crop alternating with rows of another). It makes better use of sunlight, nutrients and space, gives more yield from the same land and helps check pests and diseases. CROP ROTATION is growing different crops on the same field in a planned sequence over different seasons (e.g. a cereal followed by a pulse). It helps maintain soil fertility because different crops need and remove different nutrients, so no single nutrient is exhausted, and because leguminous (pulse) crops have root nodules with bacteria that FIX atmospheric nitrogen and enrich the soil with nitrogen for the next crop. Rotation also breaks the life-cycle of pests and diseases that are specific to one crop.
questions.explanation: Three patterns defined; rotation restores nitrogen via legumes and breaks pest cycles.

questions.question: What problems are caused by the excessive use of pesticides?
questions.answer: Pesticides (insecticides, weedicides, fungicides) protect crops but their overuse causes serious problems: (1) they pollute the soil and water; (2) they kill useful insects such as honey-bees and friendly soil organisms; (3) they leave harmful residues on food that can harm the health of consumers and farm workers; (4) pests gradually become resistant, so more pesticide is needed; and (5) harmful chemicals accumulate along the food chain. Hence pesticides must be used carefully and sparingly, and biological control should be encouraged.
questions.explanation: Pollution, killing useful organisms, residues/health harm, resistance.

questions.question: Distinguish between milch animals and draught animals, giving one example breed of milch cattle.
questions.answer: MILCH (dairy) animals are cattle kept mainly for their MILK — for example cows of the Sahiwal or Red Sindhi breed, or the Murrah buffalo. DRAUGHT animals are kept mainly for WORK such as ploughing fields, drawing carts and lifting irrigation water. A good milch breed gives a high milk yield over a long lactation period, while a good draught animal is strong and sturdy.
questions.explanation: Milch = milk (Sahiwal/Murrah); draught = work (ploughing, carts).

questions.question: Differentiate between capture fisheries and culture fisheries. What is composite fish culture?
questions.answer: CAPTURE FISHERIES means obtaining fish by CATCHING them from natural water bodies such as seas, rivers and lakes, using boats and nets. CULTURE FISHERIES (fish farming) means REARING fish under controlled conditions in ponds and tanks; rearing aquatic organisms this way is called aquaculture and rearing fish in particular is called pisciculture. COMPOSITE FISH CULTURE is a type of culture fishery in which several compatible fish species that feed at different levels of the pond (surface, middle and bottom feeders) are reared together, so that all the food available in the pond is used and a high yield is obtained from the same pond.
questions.explanation: Capture = catch from nature; culture = rear in ponds; composite = many feeding-level species together.

questions.question: What is apiculture? State two benefits of bee-keeping.
questions.answer: APICULTURE (bee-keeping) is the rearing of honey-bees in artificial hives to obtain honey and beeswax. Two benefits: (1) it provides HONEY (a nutritious, easily digestible food also used in medicine) and beeswax, giving extra income to farmers at low cost; (2) while collecting nectar, the bees POLLINATE the flowers of nearby crops and fruit trees, which increases the yield of those crops.
questions.explanation: Definition + honey/wax income and pollination of crops.

questions.question: What is food preservation? Describe any four common methods of preserving food.
questions.answer: FOOD PRESERVATION means treating and storing food so that it does not spoil and can be kept for a longer time. Food spoils mainly because of micro-organisms (bacteria, fungi, yeasts), enzymes, moisture and air. Four common methods: (1) DRYING (dehydration) — removing water from food (drying grains, pulses, fish; making raisins from grapes) so micro-organisms cannot grow without moisture. (2) SALTING/SUGARING — adding salt or sugar draws water out of the food and microbes, preventing growth (pickles, salted fish, jams). (3) CANNING — cooking food, sealing it in airtight cans or bottles and heating to kill micro-organisms, so it keeps for a long time. (4) REFRIGERATION AND FREEZING — storing food at low temperature slows microbial growth and enzyme action, keeping milk, vegetables, meat and fish fresh.
questions.explanation: Definition + drying, salting, canning, refrigeration explained with examples.

questions.question: Why is there a need to increase food production?
questions.answer: India's population keeps growing, so the demand for food rises every year, but the land available for farming is limited and even shrinking. Therefore food output must be increased mainly by raising the yield (productivity) per hectare using improved varieties, fertilisers, irrigation and crop protection.
questions.explanation: Growing population + limited land → raise yield per hectare.

questions.question: What is the Green Revolution?
questions.answer: The Green Revolution is the large increase in food-grain (mainly wheat and rice) production in India from the 1960s, achieved by using high-yielding varieties of seeds along with chemical fertilisers, assured irrigation and modern machinery. It made India self-sufficient in cereals.
questions.explanation: HYVs + fertilisers + irrigation → self-sufficiency in grains.

questions.question: Name the White Revolution and the Blue Revolution.
questions.answer: The WHITE REVOLUTION (Operation Flood) refers to the large increase in MILK production in India through better dairy farming and cattle breeds. The BLUE REVOLUTION refers to the large increase in FISH production through improved fisheries and aquaculture.
questions.explanation: White = milk; Blue = fish.

questions.question: What is hybridisation?
questions.answer: Hybridisation is the crossing of two genetically different but desirable parent plants so that the offspring (hybrid) combines the good qualities of both, such as high yield, disease resistance and drought tolerance. It is a main method of producing improved crop varieties.
questions.explanation: Crossing desirable parents to combine good traits.

questions.question: What do the letters N, P and K stand for in plant nutrition?
questions.answer: N stands for NITROGEN, P stands for PHOSPHORUS and K stands for POTASSIUM. These are the three macronutrients that plants need in the largest amounts, and they are supplied through manures and fertilisers.
questions.explanation: Nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium = NPK macronutrients.

questions.question: List three desirable features of an improved crop variety.
questions.answer: An improved variety should have: (1) HIGH YIELD — more produce per unit area; (2) RESISTANCE to diseases and pests; (3) TOLERANCE to drought, flooding or other stress; and (4) EARLY MATURITY, so that more crops can be grown in a year, along with good nutritional quality. (Any three.)
questions.explanation: High yield, disease resistance, stress tolerance, early maturity.

questions.question: State two advantages and one disadvantage of manures.
questions.answer: Advantages of manures: (1) they add HUMUS, which improves soil texture, water-holding capacity and aeration and encourages useful soil micro-organisms; (2) they are cheap, use up farm waste and are environmentally friendly. Disadvantage: they contain only small amounts of nutrients, so large quantities must be applied to meet the crop's needs.
questions.explanation: Adds humus/eco-friendly vs nutrient-poor.

questions.question: State two advantages and one disadvantage of chemical fertilisers.
questions.answer: Advantages of fertilisers: (1) they are rich in nutrients, so a small quantity gives a large effect and quick high yield; (2) they are easy to store, transport and apply. Disadvantage: they are costly and, if used continuously without manure, they damage soil structure, reduce fertility and pollute water bodies (eutrophication).
questions.explanation: Nutrient-rich/quick yield vs costly/polluting.

questions.question: Why is a balanced use of both manures and fertilisers recommended?
questions.answer: Manures alone supply few nutrients but keep the SOIL healthy by adding humus and supporting soil organisms; fertilisers alone give quick high yields but, used continuously, harm soil structure and pollute water. Using BOTH together combines the benefits: manures maintain soil fertility and structure for the long term, while fertilisers meet the crop's immediate high nutrient demand. This gives good yield without degrading the soil — a sustainable approach.
questions.explanation: Manures keep soil healthy; fertilisers give yield; both together are sustainable.

questions.question: Differentiate between kharif and rabi crops.
questions.answer: Kharif crops are sown at the start of the monsoon (June–July) and harvested in September–October; examples are rice, maize and cotton. Rabi crops are sown in winter (October–November) and harvested in spring (March–April); examples are wheat, gram and mustard.
questions.explanation: Kharif = monsoon-sown; rabi = winter-sown.

questions.question: What is mixed cropping? How does it help the farmer?
questions.answer: Mixed cropping is growing two or more crops together on the same field at the same time (for example wheat with gram). It helps the farmer by reducing the risk of total failure — if one crop fails due to pests or weather, the other crop may still give a yield. It also makes better use of land.
questions.explanation: Two crops together; reduces risk of total failure.

questions.question: What is crop rotation and how does it maintain soil fertility?
questions.answer: Crop rotation is growing different crops on the same field in a planned sequence over different seasons. It maintains soil fertility because different crops draw different nutrients, so no single nutrient is exhausted; and because growing a leguminous (pulse) crop, whose root nodules fix atmospheric nitrogen, enriches the soil with nitrogen for the next cereal crop. Rotation also breaks the life-cycle of pests and diseases.
questions.explanation: Different crops in sequence; legumes fix nitrogen; breaks pest cycles.

questions.question: Compare drip and sprinkler irrigation.
questions.answer: In DRIP irrigation water is delivered drop by drop directly to the roots through narrow tubes; it saves the most water and is ideal for orchards and water-scarce regions. In SPRINKLER irrigation water is sprayed over the field like rain through nozzles; it is useful on sandy or uneven land. Both are water-saving methods compared with flooding the field.
questions.explanation: Drip = drops to roots (most saving); sprinkler = rain-like spray.

questions.question: What are weeds? How are they controlled?
questions.answer: Weeds are unwanted plants that grow along with the crop and compete with it for water, nutrients, light and space, thereby reducing yield. They are controlled mechanically (by hand-weeding, hoeing and ploughing) and chemically (by spraying weedicides such as 2,4-D).
questions.explanation: Unwanted competing plants; mechanical + chemical (weedicide) control.

questions.question: Name three causes of plant diseases and one way to control them.
questions.answer: Plant diseases are caused by pathogens such as BACTERIA, FUNGI and VIRUSES, present in the soil, water or air. They can be controlled by using disease-resistant varieties, treating seeds before sowing, and spraying fungicides/pesticides.
questions.explanation: Bacteria, fungi, viruses; control by resistant varieties/fungicides.

questions.question: List three problems caused by the excessive use of pesticides.
questions.answer: Excessive pesticide use: (1) pollutes the soil and water; (2) kills useful insects such as honey-bees and friendly soil organisms; (3) leaves harmful residues on food, harming the health of consumers and farm workers; and (4) makes pests resistant over time. (Any three.) Hence pesticides must be used carefully and sparingly.
questions.explanation: Pollution, killing useful organisms, harmful residues, resistance.

questions.question: How should grains be stored to prevent losses?
questions.answer: Harvested grain should first be DRIED to a low moisture content, then cleaned and stored in clean, dry, airtight containers, godowns or silos. Fumigants are used to kill insect pests, and the store is protected from rodents and dampness. This prevents losses from biotic factors (insects, rodents, fungi) and abiotic factors (moisture, temperature).
questions.explanation: Dry, clean, airtight storage; fumigate; protect from pests and moisture.

questions.question: Differentiate between milch and draught animals.
questions.answer: Milch (dairy) animals are cattle reared mainly for MILK, such as Sahiwal cows or Murrah buffaloes. Draught animals are reared mainly for WORK such as ploughing fields, drawing carts and lifting irrigation water. A good milch animal gives a high milk yield, while a good draught animal is strong and sturdy.
questions.explanation: Milch = milk; draught = work.

questions.question: What are roughage and concentrates in cattle fodder?
questions.answer: Cattle fodder has two parts. ROUGHAGE is the fibre-rich part such as hay, straw and green grass, which provides bulk and fibre. CONCENTRATES are the nutrient-rich part such as oil cakes, grains and pulses, which provide protein and energy. A balanced diet contains both.
questions.explanation: Roughage = fibre (hay/straw); concentrates = nutrient-rich (oil cakes/grains).

questions.question: Differentiate between layers and broilers in poultry.
questions.answer: LAYERS are poultry birds reared mainly for EGGS; they need a nutrient-rich diet for steady egg production. BROILERS are poultry birds reared mainly for MEAT; they are given protein- and fat-rich feed so that they grow quickly to marketable weight.
questions.explanation: Layers = eggs; broilers = meat.

questions.question: What management practices keep cattle healthy and productive?
questions.answer: Healthy, productive cattle need: (1) clean, well-ventilated, dry SHELTERS that protect them from heat, cold and rain; (2) a BALANCED DIET of fodder containing both roughage (fibre) and concentrates (nutrients); (3) clean drinking water and regular grooming/brushing for hygiene; and (4) disease PREVENTION through vaccination, deworming and prompt veterinary treatment. Good breeds (or cross-breeds) further improve milk yield.
questions.explanation: Clean shelter, balanced fodder, hygiene, vaccination, good breeds.

questions.question: What is the difference between capture and culture fisheries?
questions.answer: Capture fisheries means CATCHING fish from natural water bodies such as seas, rivers and lakes using boats and nets. Culture fisheries (fish farming) means REARING fish under controlled conditions in ponds and tanks, also called aquaculture/pisciculture.
questions.explanation: Capture = catch from nature; culture = rear in ponds.

questions.question: What is composite fish culture and why is it useful?
questions.answer: Composite fish culture is a method of culture fishery in which several compatible fish species that feed at DIFFERENT levels of the pond — surface feeders, middle feeders and bottom feeders — are reared together in the same pond. It is useful because all the food available at every level of the pond is used up by some species, so there is no waste and a much higher total fish yield is obtained from the same pond.
questions.explanation: Many feeding-level species together → full use of pond food → high yield.

questions.question: What is apiculture? Why are bees useful to farmers?
questions.answer: Apiculture (bee-keeping) is the rearing of honey-bees in artificial hives to obtain honey and beeswax. Bees are useful because they give honey (a nutritious food and medicine) and wax, and because while collecting nectar they POLLINATE the flowers of nearby crops and fruit trees, which increases the yield of those crops.
questions.explanation: Bee-keeping for honey/wax; bees pollinate and raise crop yield.

questions.question: Name two products obtained from bee-keeping and one Indian bee commonly reared.
questions.answer: Two products from bee-keeping are HONEY (a nutritious, easily digestible food, also used in medicine) and BEESWAX (used in many products such as polishes and candles). The Italian bee (Apis mellifera) is commonly reared for its high honey yield and gentle nature; Apis cerana indica is also reared in India.
questions.explanation: Honey and wax; Apis mellifera (Italian bee).

questions.question: What is organic farming?
questions.answer: Organic farming is a system of farming that avoids or greatly limits synthetic fertilisers and pesticides and instead uses organic manures (compost, farmyard manure, vermicompost, green manure), bio-fertilisers, biological pest control and crop rotation. It keeps the soil fertile and produces chemical-free food while protecting the environment.
questions.explanation: Farming without synthetic chemicals; uses manures and bio-control.

questions.question: What is sustainable agriculture? Why is it important?
questions.answer: Sustainable agriculture is farming that produces enough food for present needs WITHOUT damaging the environment or reducing the ability of future generations to grow food. It is important because heavy use of chemicals raises yields now but degrades soil, pollutes water and harms health in the long run. Sustainable methods — crop rotation, integrated pest management, water conservation and organic manures — keep the soil, water and ecosystem healthy so that good harvests can continue for the future.
questions.explanation: Feeding the present without harming future food production; protects soil/water/health.

questions.question: Describe three methods of food preservation.
questions.answer: (1) DRYING (dehydration): removing water from food (drying grains, fish; making raisins) so that micro-organisms cannot grow without moisture. (2) SALTING/SUGARING: adding salt or sugar draws water out of the food and microbes, preventing spoilage (pickles, salted fish, jams). (3) REFRIGERATION/FREEZING: keeping food cold slows microbial growth and enzyme action, keeping milk, vegetables and meat fresh. (Canning is a fourth method.)
questions.explanation: Drying, salting, refrigeration explained with examples.

questions.question: Why does food spoil, and how does canning prevent it?
questions.answer: Food spoils mainly because of the action of micro-organisms (bacteria, fungi, yeasts), enzymes, moisture and air. CANNING prevents spoilage by cooking the food, sealing it in airtight cans or bottles, and heating it to kill the micro-organisms present; the airtight seal then keeps out fresh air and microbes, so the food keeps for a long time.
questions.explanation: Microbes/enzymes cause spoilage; canning kills microbes and seals out air.

questions.question: How does salting help to preserve food such as fish or pickles?
questions.answer: Adding common salt (or sugar) draws water OUT of the food and out of the cells of any micro-organisms present, by osmosis. Because micro-organisms cannot grow without water, the high salt (or sugar) concentration stops their growth and so prevents the food from spoiling. This is how salted fish, pickles and jams are preserved.
questions.explanation: Salt draws out water by osmosis; microbes cannot grow without water.

questions.question: A farmer's field has been giving lower yields every year. A soil scientist tells him the soil has lost its organic matter and is low in nitrogen, and that he has been using only urea for ten years. (a) Why has continuous use of only urea reduced his soil fertility? (b) What single nutrient does urea mainly supply? (c) Suggest two things the farmer should do to improve the soil.
questions.answer: (a) Using only a chemical fertiliser such as urea for many years supplies nutrients to the crop but adds NO organic matter (humus) to the soil; over time the soil structure breaks down, useful soil organisms decline and fertility falls. (b) Urea mainly supplies NITROGEN. (c) The farmer should (i) add organic MANURE or compost to restore humus and soil structure, and (ii) practise CROP ROTATION with a leguminous (pulse) crop that fixes atmospheric nitrogen — and use a balance of manures and fertilisers rather than fertiliser alone.
questions.explanation: Fertiliser-only farming removes humus; balance with manure + legume rotation.

questions.question: Two farmers grow the same crop. Farmer A uses only large amounts of chemical fertiliser; Farmer B uses a mixture of compost and a moderate amount of fertiliser. After five years, Farmer A's soil is hard and his nearby pond is full of algae, while Farmer B's soil is soft and fertile. (a) Why is Farmer A's pond full of algae? (b) Why is Farmer B's soil better? (c) Which approach is more sustainable and why?
questions.answer: (a) Excess chemical fertiliser from Farmer A's field is washed by rain into the pond; the extra nutrients cause an over-growth of algae — a process called eutrophication. (b) Farmer B adds COMPOST (organic manure), which supplies humus that improves soil texture, water-holding capacity and aeration and supports useful soil organisms, keeping the soil soft and fertile. (c) Farmer B's approach (a balance of manure and fertiliser) is more SUSTAINABLE because it gives good yields while maintaining long-term soil health and avoiding water pollution, whereas Farmer A's fertiliser-only method degrades soil and pollutes water.
questions.explanation: Runoff causes eutrophication; manure keeps soil healthy; balanced use is sustainable.

questions.question: A farmer in a region with little rainfall wants to grow wheat in winter and make the best use of his limited water and land. (a) In which season (kharif/rabi) does wheat grow? (b) Which water-saving irrigation method should he choose and why? (c) Suggest one cropping pattern that would reduce his risk of crop failure.
questions.answer: (a) Wheat is a RABI (winter) crop, sown in October–November and harvested in March–April. (b) He should choose DRIP irrigation, because it delivers water drop by drop directly to the roots and wastes the least water, which is ideal in a low-rainfall, water-scarce region (a sprinkler system would be a second choice). (c) He could use MIXED CROPPING (for example wheat with gram) or CROP ROTATION so that if one crop fails due to lack of water or pests, the other crop may still give a yield, reducing his risk.
questions.explanation: Wheat = rabi; drip saves water; mixed cropping/rotation reduces risk.

questions.question: A farmer sprays heavy doses of the same insecticide on his cotton crop every season. At first the pests die, but after a few years the same insecticide no longer works, his honey-bee visitors have disappeared, and a stream near the field has dead fish. (a) Why does the insecticide no longer kill the pests? (b) Why have the honey-bees disappeared? (c) Why are there dead fish in the stream? (d) Suggest one safer practice.
questions.answer: (a) Repeated use of the SAME insecticide makes the pests develop RESISTANCE — the few survivors breed and pass on resistance, so the chemical stops working. (b) The insecticide kills useful insects too, including the honey-BEES that visited the crop. (c) The insecticide has been washed into the stream, polluting the water and KILLING the fish (and accumulating in the food chain). (d) Safer practices: use insecticides sparingly and only when needed, rotate different chemicals, grow pest-resistant varieties, and use BIOLOGICAL pest control (natural predators) / integrated pest management.
questions.explanation: Resistance, harm to bees, water pollution killing fish; use IPM/biological control.

questions.question: After harvest, a farmer stores his wheat in damp jute sacks in an open shed during the rainy season. Within weeks the grain develops fungus and is attacked by insects and rats, and much of it is spoilt. (a) Name one biotic and one abiotic factor responsible for the loss. (b) What should the farmer have done to the grain before storing it? (c) Describe the correct way to store the grain.
questions.answer: (a) Biotic factor: insects, rats (rodents) and fungi attacking the grain. Abiotic factor: high MOISTURE (dampness) and unsuitable temperature during the rainy season. (b) Before storage the grain should have been properly DRIED to reduce its moisture content (and cleaned). (c) The dried, cleaned grain should be stored in clean, DRY, AIRTIGHT containers, godowns or silos, protected from rats and dampness, and treated with fumigants to kill any insect pests.
questions.explanation: Biotic (insects/rats/fungi) + abiotic (moisture); dry first; airtight clean storage.

questions.question: A dairy farmer keeps cows in a dark, crowded, damp shed, feeds them only dry straw, and does not vaccinate them. His milk yield is low and the cows often fall ill. (a) Give two faults in his management. (b) What is wrong with feeding only straw? (c) Suggest two improvements to raise milk yield and keep the cows healthy.
questions.answer: (a) Two faults: the shed is dark, crowded and damp (poor, unhygienic housing that spreads disease), and the cows are NOT vaccinated (so they catch diseases). (b) Straw is only ROUGHAGE (fibre); feeding only straw means the cows do not get enough nutrients — they also need CONCENTRATES (oil cakes, grains) rich in protein and energy for good milk production. (c) Improvements: provide clean, dry, well-ventilated shelter and a BALANCED diet of roughage plus concentrates with clean water; vaccinate and deworm the cows regularly; groom them; and use good milch breeds or cross-breeds for higher yield.
questions.explanation: Bad housing + no vaccination; straw alone lacks nutrients; provide shelter, balanced feed, vaccination, good breeds.

questions.question: A village has a large unused pond and many flowering mustard fields nearby. A self-help group wants to earn extra income. (a) Suggest how they can use the pond for food production and name the practice. (b) How can rearing several fish species together increase their yield? (c) Suggest how they can also use the mustard fields to earn income while helping the crop, and name that practice.
questions.answer: (a) They can rear fish in the pond — culture fishery / pisciculture (aquaculture). (b) By practising COMPOSITE FISH CULTURE — rearing several compatible species that feed at different levels of the pond (surface, middle and bottom feeders) together — all the food available in the pond is used, so the total fish yield is much higher. (c) Near the mustard fields they can set up bee-hives (APICULTURE / bee-keeping). The bees give honey and wax for sale, and while collecting nectar they POLLINATE the mustard flowers, increasing the mustard yield — so both the bee-keepers and the crop benefit.
questions.explanation: Pisciculture + composite fish culture for high yield; apiculture gives honey and pollinates mustard.

questions.question: A family buys fresh fish, grapes, and milk, and wants to keep each for as long as possible without it spoiling. (a) Why does food spoil? (b) Suggest a suitable preservation method for each item and explain how it works. (c) Name one method that uses high temperature and one that uses low temperature.
questions.answer: (a) Food spoils mainly because of the growth of micro-organisms (bacteria, fungi, yeasts) and the action of enzymes, helped by moisture, air and warmth. (b) FISH can be preserved by DRYING or SALTING (removing/binding water so microbes cannot grow) or by freezing; GRAPES can be preserved by DRYING them into raisins (removing moisture); MILK can be preserved by REFRIGERATION (and by boiling/pasteurisation), which slows microbial growth. (c) A method using HIGH temperature is canning/pasteurisation (heating kills microbes); a method using LOW temperature is refrigeration or freezing.
questions.explanation: Microbes/enzymes spoil food; dry/salt fish, dry grapes, refrigerate milk; canning = heat, refrigeration = cold.

questions.question: Between 1947 and the 1960s India often imported food grains. From the late 1960s, production rose sharply and India became self-sufficient in cereals. (a) Name the change in agriculture responsible for this rise. (b) List three components of this change. (c) Why could simply farming more land not have solved the food problem?
questions.answer: (a) The change was the GREEN REVOLUTION. (b) Three components: high-yielding varieties (HYVs) of seeds, chemical fertilisers, and assured irrigation (also modern machinery and pesticides). (c) Simply farming more land could not solve the problem because good agricultural land is LIMITED and is shrinking due to towns and industry; the only lasting solution was to raise the YIELD per hectare (productivity) through scientific methods, which is what the Green Revolution achieved.
questions.explanation: Green Revolution; HYVs + fertilisers + irrigation; limited land means raise yield per hectare.

questions.question: A farmer grows only wheat on the same field season after season. Over time the soil's nitrogen falls, pests that attack wheat increase, and his yields drop. (a) Name the cropping practice that would solve this and define it. (b) Which type of crop should he include to restore soil nitrogen and why? (c) State one more benefit of this practice.
questions.answer: (a) The practice is CROP ROTATION — growing different crops on the same field in a planned sequence across seasons instead of the same crop repeatedly. (b) He should include a LEGUMINOUS (pulse) crop such as gram or pea, because legumes have root nodules containing bacteria that FIX atmospheric nitrogen and enrich the soil with nitrogen for the next crop. (c) Another benefit: crop rotation breaks the life-cycle of pests and diseases specific to wheat, so their build-up is reduced; it also uses soil nutrients more evenly.
questions.explanation: Crop rotation; include a legume to fix nitrogen; also breaks pest cycles.
